title: The chapter of eights
hookLine: sixteen short poems against clinging to views

lines: WHAT HAPPENS TO THE ONE WHO NEEDS TO BE?
cards: An argument online: two people, each certain, each quoting, each getting louder. Neither one changes the other's mind, and both log off a little more sure they were right.
A set of old poems looks at that exact scene and asks a strange question. Not who's right. What happens to a person who needs to be?
That's the fourth chapter of the Sutta Nipata: sixteen short poems with a curious name, the Atthakavagga, the chapter of eights.

teach.b: Atthaka means a group of eight, and vagga means a chapter.
The name probably comes from several of its poems that have eight verses each: the eights on the cave, on the corrupted, on the pure, on the supreme. Not all sixteen do.
Some scholars count this chapter among the early layers of Buddhist verse, partly because other parts of the canon know it by name.

In the Udana, a monk named Sona is invited to recite, and he chants all sixteen poems of the eights from memory; the Buddha praises how well he has learned them. In that story, the poems are already a set, known by heart.
And what do they say? Again and again, the same thing from different sides. People hold a view and call it the best.
They call everyone else's foolish. They go into the assembly to argue, hungry for praise, and if they lose, they're stung.

teach.h: THE SAGE DOESN'T ENTER THE RING.
teach.b: The sage, the poems say, doesn't step into that ring.
Not because he has a cleverer view, but because he doesn't grasp any view as the thing that makes him pure.
Some lines are hard, and teachers read them in different ways: does the sage hold no views at all, or hold them lightly? The poems themselves leave room for both.

how: The Atthakavagga is studied in Theravada monasteries and widely read by lay Buddhists and scholars for its early style; teachers often draw on it when speaking about letting go of attachment to views.

games.q: the chapter of eights: tap the pairs.

s: every poem in the Atthakavagga has exactly eight verses
only some do; the name probably comes from those.
another book of the canon tells of a monk reciting these poems
in the Udana, Sona chants the poems of the eights and the Buddha praises him.
the poems say the sage wins debates with the cleverest view
they say the sage doesn't enter the contest of views at all.

games.q: two teachers are debating in the assembly, each calling his own view the purest. you're the sage the Atthakavagga describes. what do you do?
o: join in with a better argument.
stay out of it, holding no view as what makes you pure.
games.why: the poems' sage doesn't step into the dispute; it's grasping at a view as purifying that he lets go of.

practice: Bring to mind one opinion you hold strongly, not to drop it, only to notice how it sits in the body when you think of someone who disagrees: the jaw, the chest, the hands. Notice the wanting to win.
Then let the breath soften that place, and let the opinion simply be an opinion, held in an open hand.

wordCard.voice: Atthakavagga. The chapter of eights, the fourth chapter of the Sutta Nipata: sixteen short, old poems on not clinging to views.
